summary.text:
Not a council to write to in the ordinary way, and the report knows it. Thurrock cannot balance its budget without a capitalisation direction; £52.2m of treasury costs sit inside an estimated £59.1m annual deficit, and the direction that funds the deficit becomes CFR and attracts further MRP and interest. Non-HRA financing costs are 35.2% of net revenue stream. The commissioners' own comment calls the position unsustainable.

The balance sheet reconciles: CFR £1,071m less gross debt of £876m gives the £195m of under-borrowing they state. Government has committed in principle to repaying £200m of non-HRA debt during 2026/27, announced 25 March 2026, and the debt pool is being split into HRA and non-HRA from 1 April 2026 to make that possible.

The treasury point is the 75%. Three-quarters of the external debt is short-term, held there on MHCLG discussions, expected receipts and 'the expectation of a fall in interest rates'. Paragraph 13 records what happened instead: MUFG's forecast fall to 4.80% on long PWLB became a rise above 6%. Their own risk register scores both interest rate risk and refinancing risk Amber, and £665m of the £845m PWLB book is short-dated. No officer email address is published anywhere in the report.

contacts.note: Named without addresses: Richard Dunlop (Interim Treasury Manager), David McNamara (Director of Finance/Deputy S151), Cllr S Poyntz (Cabinet Member for Finance).

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the treasury report going to Audit Committee on 14 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

We'll keep this to mechanics. Your report sets out the budget position at length and it is not our place to add anything to it.

A cross-check first. CFR of £1,071m less gross debt of £876m gives the £195m of under-borrowing you state at 9.4 — exact. We hold 28 PWLB loans at a balance of £821.1m against the £845m of PWLB you show at 1 April 2026, the gap being the four months between our file and your date.

The reason we wrote is paragraph 14.3 read next to the £200m. Government committed in principle on 25 March to repaying £200m of non-HRA debt during 2026/27, with formal approval and detailed implementation still to come, and the debt pool is being split into HRA and non-HRA from 1 April 2026 to make it possible. Which £200m it is has a large and computable effect, because your book is really two books.

On the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, notice 314/26, six of your loans — £160.9m of principal — carry about £49.9m of discount between them. The other twenty we can price, £660.2m of short-dated money, sit about £2.1m in premium, which is to say essentially at par. So the long sixth of the book is worth substantially less than face and the short three-quarters is worth roughly face. If the composition of the £200m is still open, that difference is worth knowing before it is settled rather than after. We compute it every morning for every council and yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Ours is indicative; the DMO's is the only quote that binds, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment.

The second thing is your paragraph 13, and we raise it because it is the clearest statement of the problem we are built to address that we have read in a council paper. You record MUFG's long-term view as Bank Rate falling to 3.5% with long PWLB rates falling to 4.80%, and then note what actually happened: "longer term fixed PWLB interest rates have risen above 6%, rather than the forecasted fall to 4.80%." Meanwhile 75% of the external debt is short-term, held there partly on "the expectation of a fall in interest rates".

We do not publish forecasts, and that is deliberate. What we publish is the market's own implied path — the SONIA/OIS curve, updated daily, which tells you what rates are actually priced rather than what anyone expects. As of this afternoon Bank Rate is 3.75%, the implied one-year is 4.11% and two-year 4.21%, and twenty-year PWLB certainty is 6.38%. That is not a better forecast than your adviser's; it is a different kind of object, and it is the one that would have shown the divergence from 4.80% as it happened rather than in the following year's report. With three-quarters of a £876m book on short-dated funding, the difference between an annual view and a daily one is not academic.

For the rollover itself: July's sector borrowing was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. A thin market matters more when you are refinancing £665m of short-term PWLB than when you are not. That is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four fit. SONIA Forward Curve & OIS and Reading the PWLBpredict are the two that speak to paragraph 13. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator for the £200m composition question. And After the S114: capitalisation & EFS. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
